subject: English
passage: Folklorist Elsa Magnusson believes that we might learn how the call-and-response epic form of the Sahelian griots first emerged if we understand why griot performers sometimes incorporate structural features borrowed from neighboring oral traditions. Magnusson and colleagues reviewed data from many studies of how griot performance responds when it encounters another type of oral tradition, including Datu Vo's work on Hausa praise-singing and Amina Bello's work on Tuareg desert poetry. Magnusson and colleagues concluded that neither Hausa praise-singing nor Tuareg desert poetry is likely to have played a significant role in the development of the griot epic form.
prompt: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Magnusson and colleagues' conclusion?

choices.A: Griot performance tended to incorporate borrowed structural features when it encountered Hausa praise-singing and when it encountered Tuareg desert poetry.
choices.B: Griot performance tended to incorporate borrowed structural features when it encountered Hausa praise-singing, but not when it encountered Tuareg desert poetry.
choices.C: Griot performance tended to incorporate borrowed structural features when it encountered Tuareg desert poetry, but not when it encountered Hausa praise-singing.
choices.D: Griot performance did not tend to incorporate borrowed structural features when it encountered either Hausa praise-singing or Tuareg desert poetry.

explanation:
Choice D is the best answer. The text explains that Magnusson is investigating why griot performers sometimes incorporate structural features borrowed from neighboring oral traditions, believing this could help explain how the call-and-response epic form first emerged. After reviewing data on how griot performance responds when it encounters Hausa praise-singing and Tuareg desert poetry, Magnusson and colleagues concluded that neither of these traditions likely played a significant role in the griot form's development. If griot performance did not tend to incorporate borrowed structural features when it encountered either tradition, this would support that conclusion, since it would suggest that neither tradition acted as a meaningful trigger for the borrowing behavior tied to the form's emergence.

Why A is incorrect:

Choice A is incorrect because finding that griot performance tended to incorporate borrowed features when it encountered both Hausa praise-singing and Tuareg desert poetry would contradict, not support, Magnusson and colleagues' conclusion. Such a finding would suggest that both neighboring traditions did trigger borrowing and therefore played a role in shaping the griot epic form.
